title: Sunshine
intro: The opening is a teacher speaking, not Jack offering advice to a struggling pupil. A minor offense becomes grounds for humiliation, threats and a demand for paid tutoring. Then a familiar school song is taken over by the child's revenge fantasy. The later rapper's voice pushes that revolt into obscene spectacle and demands an audience of its own. The song's force comes from those changes of speaker: the teacher's respectable mission conceals self-interest, while rebellion knows how to seize attention but does not suddenly acquire a gentler language. The sunshine stays cheerful through all of it.
reading: Teacher roleplay, classroom commerce, inherited playground revolt, then a performer's command; do not conflate voices.

revisions.sunshine-teacher: The first-person 'teacher, me' establishes a role that continues through the tutoring pitch. That matters when the pupil is called worthless or told to die: these are the authority figure's words, dramatized so we can hear the cruelty inside them. The initial description is only 'a little naughty.' The punishment therefore tells us more about the adult's need to dominate than about the child's offense. Jack makes the teacher condemn himself before handing the song over to the schoolyard fantasy that answers him.
revisions.editorial-3-career: The teacher finally says what the child is getting in the way of: 'my' educational undertaking. That possessive word reverses the expected relationship. Education should exist for the pupil, but the pupil now owes the teacher a successful career. The next demand for private tutoring converts that reversal into a transaction. The bad student is at once an embarrassment to be discarded and a customer who must keep paying. The verse's target is this contradiction, not simply strictness or the existence of school.
revisions.editorial-3-parents: This line joins the teacher's interest to the family's emotional pressure. He has just named the price of coming to his home; now refusal can be made to feel like betraying the parents. It is the final move in the pitch because it lets the teacher's demand travel beyond his direct supervision. The pupil is supposed to police himself through shame. When the nursery-song parody begins immediately afterward, its childishness is also a refusal to keep speaking in the adult's language of duty and investment.
revisions.phrase-3-commands: There are two steps in this refrain. 'What can't I say or do?' rejects the adult's prohibitions; 'you must listen and watch' then claims authority over the audience. The rebel wants more than escape—he wants the ability to make other people witness his power. That makes the shift to rapper's bravado feel continuous with the classroom scene even as the speaker changes. The song can expose the teacher's violence while also showing how a person answering humiliation reaches for commands and humiliation of his own.
revisions.phrase-3-pixels: The body becomes a censored or unrecognizable image, then something beyond an autopsy. This is the rapper's exaggerated horror-show vocabulary, following the demand to watch what he does. It extends the child's fantasy of making the school disappear into a fantasy of leaving nothing an observer can make sense of. The important movement is from being examined, graded and punished to imagining an act that defeats examination altogether. The cheerful school-song refrain then returns rather than offering any realistic resolution to that fantasy.
